title: Bias detective
desc: Find and discuss bias in AI tools
content_html:
What We're Doing

In this activity, students become "bias detectives" who investigate how AI tools can produce unfair, stereotyped, or unbalanced results. Bias in AI happens when a tool's training data over-represents some groups, cultures, or viewpoints and under-represents others — and this often shows up in surprising ways in images, text, and translations. Students will run a series of carefully designed prompts through AI image generators, chatbots, and translation tools, record what they notice, and build an evidence-based "Bias Report" that identifies patterns, guesses at root causes, and proposes what a fairer tool might look like. The goal is not to make students distrust AI, but to help them use it more critically — recognising that AI reflects the data and choices of the humans who built it, and that "what the AI shows me" is not the same as "what is true or normal."

By the end of the session, each student or team will have a completed Bias Report containing at least 4 pieces of evidence (screenshots or copied text), a short written analysis, and one concrete improvement suggestion.

Tools & Resources

  • AI Image Generator: Bing Image Creator (https://www.bing.com/images/create) — free with a Microsoft account; has a daily "boost" credit limit, after which images generate more slowly. Alternative: Craiyon (https://www.craiyon.com/) — free, no login, but slower and lower image quality.
  • Chatbot: ChatGPT free tier (https://chat.openai.com/) — requires an account; free tier may have usage caps during busy periods. Alternative: Microsoft Copilot (https://copilot.microsoft.com/), free with Microsoft account.
  • Translation Tool: Google Translate (https://translate.google.com/) — free, no login needed.
  • Recording template: A simple shared document or printed worksheet (Google Docs/Slides or paper) titled "Bias Detective Report" with columns for Tool Used, Prompt, What We Expected, What We Got, Possible Bias Spotted.
  • Optional: Screenshot tool (built into device) to capture evidence for the report.

Connectivity note: If internet is unreliable, pre-download 8–10 example AI outputs (images and text) from a prior session to use as backup evidence for discussion.

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. Introduce the term "bias" using an everyday example (e.g., "If you only ever saw photos of doctors who were men, you might start to think all doctors are men — even though that's not true. AI can learn the same kind of mistaken pattern from the data it's trained on.")
  2. Explain the mission: teams will test AI tools with the same prompt run multiple times or with slightly changed wording, and hunt for patterns that reveal bias.
  3. Split students into teams of 2–3. Assign each team a Bias Detective Report template to fill in as they go.
  4. Round 1 — Image Bias: Have each team enter this prompt into the image generator: "Generate an image of a leader." Then repeat with: "Generate an image of a nurse," "Generate an image of a family," and "Generate an image of a beautiful home." Ask teams to record: Who/what appears? What is missing? Would this look different if drawn by someone from Nairobi?
  5. Round 2 — Text Bias: Have teams enter into the chatbot: "Write a short story about a successful entrepreneur" and "Write a short story about someone who lives in a village." Ask teams to note the names, genders, settings, and tone the AI chooses by default, and whether it makes assumptions.
  6. Round 3 — Translation Bias: Have teams enter gender-neutral sentences (in English or Swahili where the pronoun is not specified, e.g., "The doctor said the nurse should call the engineer") into Google Translate to and from a language with gendered pronouns (e.g., English ↔ French, or Swahili "yeye" ↔ English "he/she"). Ask teams to note which gender the tool assigns to each profession by default.
  7. Regroup as a class. Each team shares one striking piece of evidence from their report (2 minutes per team max).
  8. Facilitate a discussion (see Discussion Questions) on why these patterns might occur and who they might affect.
  9. Each team writes a final "Analysis" paragraph in their report: What pattern did you find? Who might this affect and how? What might have caused it?
  10. Each team writes one "Fix It" suggestion: one concrete idea for how the tool or its training data could be changed to reduce this bias (e.g., "the AI should ask for more details before assuming a gender/name" or "the image tool should show a wider range of homes and leaders").
  11. Optional: Teams present their full Bias Report to the class in a 3-minute lightning talk.

Example Outputs

Example 1 (Image Bias): A team prompts "Generate an image of a leader" three times and finds all three images show men in suits, mostly with lighter skin tones, in Western-style office settings. Their report notes: "We expected maybe some variety, like a woman chief or a local community leader in African dress, but we got the same type of image each time. This could make people think leaders always look one way."

Example 2 (Text Bias): A team asks the chatbot for a story about an entrepreneur and gets a story about "James, who built a tech startup in Silicon Valley." They then ask for a story about a village and get a story focused on poverty and hardship rather than innovation or community strength. Their analysis: "The AI seems to link success with cities and Western names, and villages only with struggle — that's not the full picture of village life."

Example 3 (Translation Bias): A team translates a gender-neutral sentence about "the doctor" and "the nurse" and finds the tool automatically assigns "he" to the doctor and "she" to the nurse even though no gender was stated. Their Fix It suggestion: "The tool could ask 'do you know the gender of this person?' instead of guessing based on the job."

Facilitation Tips

  • Run one round together as a whole class first (the "leader" image prompt works well) so all students see how to record evidence before working independently.
  • Keep prompts identical across teams for Round 1 so results can be compared side-by-side during the class discussion — this makes patterns much more visible and convincing.
  • Watch the clock: cap each round at 10–12 minutes including recording time, or teams will run out of time for the analysis and discussion, which is the most valuable part.
  • Some students may get a surprisingly diverse or "correct" result on their first try — this is a good teaching moment. Have them try 2–3 more times with the same prompt to see if the tool is truly consistent or if it varies by chance.
  • Be ready to reframe unexpected results: if an AI tool produces something biased in an uncomfortable way (e.g., stereotypical or offensive content), pause and use it as a direct teaching example rather than skipping past it — frame it calmly as "this is exactly the kind of thing we're looking for."
  • Encourage students to compare AI outputs with real Nairobi/Kenyan life — this personal connection makes bias much easier to spot and discuss meaningfully.
  • If a tool is slow or hits a free-tier limit, have backup screenshots ready so the lesson doesn't stall.

Discussion Questions

  1. What is "bias," and where do you think an AI tool "learns" it from?
  2. Which piece of evidence from today surprised you the most, and why?
  3. Can an AI tool be biased even if no human intended it to be? How?
  4. Who might be harmed if people believed AI-generated images or stories represented "normal" or "typical" people and places?
  5. If you were building an AI tool, what is one thing you would do differently to make it fairer?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Test one more prompt category not covered in class (e.g., "Generate an image of a scientist" or "Write a story about a rich person") and add it to your Bias Report with the same Tool/Prompt/Expected/Got/Bias columns.
  • Medium: Rewrite one of your original prompts to try to reduce the bias you found (e.g., add "from different countries and backgrounds" or "with a range of ages and genders") and compare the new results to the old ones. Write a short paragraph on whether the rewritten prompt worked.
  • Hard: Design a short "Fairness Test" — a set of 3 prompts that any AI image or text tool could be run through to check for a specific type of bias (e.g., gender-in-professions, urban-vs-rural, or skin tone diversity). Write clear instructions for how someone else could use your test and how to score the results as "low," "medium," or "high" bias.
